courses.summary: Discovery, major sites, urban planning, crafts, trade, script and decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with measurement labs and the debates scholars still hold.
outcomes: Name major Harappan sites and what each shows

scenes.text: Archaeologists noticed identical seals and bricks at two far-apart sites.
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.body: Harappa was excavated from 1921 (Daya Ram Sahni) and Mohenjo-daro from 1922 (R. D. Banerji) under John Marshall, then Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (founded 1861). The mature phase is dated roughly **2600–1900 BCE**; the civilisation spread over more than a million km² across present Pakistan, north-west India and Afghanistan.

steps.title: Sites
steps.body: **Mohenjo-daro** (Sindh; Great Bath), **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan), **Dholavira** (Gujarat; water-conservation system; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021), **Lothal** (Gujarat; dockyard-like structure, bead-making), **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan; fire altars, ploughed field), **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana; one of the largest), **Banawali**.

steps.title: Terminology
steps.body: 'Harappan' and 'Indus Valley' are used interchangeably; many sites lie away from the Indus.

scenes.text: Bricks across sites share proportions.

steps.title: Planning
steps.body: Grid streets, a raised citadel and lower town, covered drains, standardised fired bricks with proportion about **4 : 2 : 1** (e.g. 28 × 14 × 7 cm), weights in a binary-decimal series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, then 160, 320, 640…).

steps.title: Calculate
steps.body: A brick of 28 × 14 × 7 cm has volume 28 × 14 × 7 = **2,744 cm³**.

steps.title: Great Bath
steps.body: About 12 m × 7 m with a depth of about 2.4 m (approximate) — a volume of ~200 m³, i.e. ~200,000 litres. Its purpose is debated: ritual bathing is commonly proposed.

scenes.text: A steatite seal shows a bull and signs of the Indus script.
Still undeciphered.

steps.title: Economy
steps.body: Agriculture (wheat, barley, cotton), crafts (carnelian beads, shell, copper and bronze), long-distance trade with Mesopotamia ('Meluhha' in cuneiform records), sea trade through Lothal and Gulf ports. No clear palaces or temples; political organisation is debated.

steps.title: Script
steps.body: About 400 signs on seals; no bilingual text; **undeciphered**. Claims of decipherment are not accepted by the scholarly community.

steps.title: Decline (c. 1900 BCE on)
steps.body: Proposed factors: shifting monsoons and drying of the Ghaggar–Hakra river system, river shifts, declining trade, regional reorganisation; no single cause is established, and cities declined unevenly over centuries. Relationship to later cultures and Indo-Aryan origins remains debated; ancient-DNA studies (e.g. Rakhigarhi 2019) are interpreted differently by scholars.

steps.title: Survey
steps.body: Pedestrian survey, remote sensing (satellite, LiDAR), magnetometry and ground-penetrating radar find sites without digging.

steps.title: Excavation
steps.body: Mortimer Wheeler (Director-General ASI 1944–48) promoted grid-based stratigraphic excavation in India. **Law of superposition**: in undisturbed deposits the lower layer is older. Record each **context** (layer, cut, fill), the position (3D), photographs and drawings; excavation is destructive, so records are the lasting evidence.

steps.title: Disturbance
steps.body: Burrowing, pits and later digging can mix layers.

scenes.text: A lab reports 25% of the original carbon-14 remains.
Half-life of C-14 is 5,730 years.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Living things take up C-14; after death it decays: N = N₀ × (½)^(t/5730). Age t = 5730 × ln(N₀/N) / ln 2. Results are **calibrated** to calendar years using records such as IntCal because atmospheric C-14 has varied. Useful to about 50,000 years.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 25% remaining = two half-lives: t = 2 × 5,730 = **11,460 years** before present (BP; 'present' = 1950).

activity.prompt: Age (years) of a sample with 25% C-14 remaining

scenes.text: Thermoluminescence measures trapped electrons since pottery was last heated.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Relative**: stratigraphy, seriation, typology. **Absolute**: **dendrochronology** (tree rings; exact years), **thermoluminescence/OSL** (last heating or light exposure), **potassium–argon / argon–argon** (volcanic layers, millions of years), **uranium-series**. Choose the method by material and age range.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Obtain permits, share findings, care for human remains respectfully, fight the antiquities trade (UNESCO 1970 Convention), consult descendant communities. India: Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1958 and Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body: Stabilise, document and store finds correctly.

steps.title: Answers

courses.title: Linguistics I · sounds, words and sentences
courses.summary: Phonetics and phonology, morphology, syntax and semantics, with Panini and Chomsky and hands-on analysis problems.
outcomes: Transcribe sounds and identify phonemes with minimal pairs
Segment words into morphemes
Draw simple phrase-structure trees
Explain Panini's place in linguistics

scenes.text: Changing /p/ to /b/ changes the meaning.
A minimal pair shows phonemes.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Phonetics**: physical sounds (place and manner of articulation, voicing). **Phonology**: sound patterns. A **phoneme** is a contrastive sound; **allophones** are variants (aspirated [pʰ] in 'pin' vs plain [p] in 'spin' in English). **Minimal pair**: words differing by one sound ('pat'/'bat'). The **IPA** transcribes sounds.

steps.title: Panini
steps.body: *Ashtadhyayi* (c. 4th–5th century BCE; about 4,000 rules) is a precise generative description of Sanskrit; its economy and rule ordering influenced later linguistics (Bloomfield, Chomsky).

steps.title: Counting
steps.body: A CV-only language with 8 consonants and 5 vowels has 8 × 5 = 40 possible syllables (like Hawaiian).

activity.prompt: A language has 8 consonants and 5 vowels, only CV syllables. How many possible syllables?

scenes.text: Un + break + able.
Words and sentences have structure.

steps.title: Morphology
steps.body: A **morpheme** is the smallest meaning-bearing unit: *un-*, *break*, *-able*. Inflection (plural -s, tense -ed) vs derivation (*happy* → *unhappy*). Agglutinative languages (Tamil, Turkish) string many suffixes; Hindi is more fusional.

steps.title: Syntax
steps.body: **Chomsky**, *Syntactic Structures* (1957): generative grammar. Phrase-structure: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP. Word order: English SVO; Hindi, Tamil and Japanese SOV.

steps.title: Tree
steps.body: 'The cat chased the mouse': [S [NP The cat] [VP chased [NP the mouse]]].

scenes.text: You are not asking about ability.
Pragmatics: meaning in context.

steps.title: Semantics
steps.body: Meaning of words and sentences: synonymy, antonymy, polysemy, entailment ('John killed Bill' entails 'Bill died').

steps.title: Pragmatics
steps.body: **Grice's maxims** (1975): Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner; speakers cooperate and imply more than they say (**implicature**). **Speech acts** (Austin, Searle): promising, requesting, warning.

steps.title: Politeness
steps.body: Indirect requests are common across languages; politeness norms differ by culture.

scenes.text: Gloss a short sentence.

steps.body: Word → morphemes → gloss → free translation, then note word order and agreement.

steps.title: Transcription
steps.body: Use IPA or a consistent romanisation.

courses.title: Linguistics II · language families, society and the languages of India
courses.summary: Language families, historical linguistics, India's linguistic diversity, multilingualism, language policy and endangerment, treated neutrally.
outcomes: Name India's major language families and give sample members
Explain the comparative method and Sir William Jones's insight

scenes.text: In 1786 Sir William Jones noted their striking affinities.
Comparative method.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Comparing regular sound correspondences (e.g. *pitar*, *pater*, *father*) to reconstruct proto-languages. Indo-European includes Sanskrit, Hindi, Persian, Greek, Latin, English. Grimm's law explains regular Germanic shifts.

steps.title: India's families
steps.body: **Indo-European (Indo-Aryan)**: Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi…; **Dravidian**: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Brahui…; **Austroasiatic**: Santali, Mundari, Khasi; **Sino-Tibetan**: Manipuri (Meitei), Bodo, Naga languages; plus isolates (Burushaski, Nihali). The Indian linguistic area shows shared features (retroflex consonants, SOV order) across families (Emeneau, 1956).

steps.title: Origins debate
steps.body: The homeland of Indo-European and the arrival of Indo-Aryan languages in India are debated: most historical linguists propose migration from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, while some scholars argue for indigenous origin; evidence from linguistics, archaeology and genetics is weighed differently.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: Constitution's Eighth Schedule: **22 languages**. Census 2011: 121 languages (22 scheduled + 99 non-scheduled) and about 19,500 raw mother-tongue names rationalised to 1,369. Hindi as mother tongue: about **52.8 crore** of 121.1 crore = 43.6%.

steps.title: Caution
steps.body: 'Hindi' in the Census groups many related varieties (e.g. Bhojpuri, Rajasthani), a point of debate among linguists and speakers.

scenes.text: The shopkeeper uses Kannada, Hindi, Tamil and English in a day.
Everyday multilingualism.

steps.title: Policy
steps.body: Articles 343–351: Hindi in Devanagari is the Union's official language and English continues as an associate official language; states choose their own. Linguistic reorganisation of states followed the 1953 Andhra state creation (after Potti Sriramulu's fast) and the States Reorganisation Act 1956. The **three-language formula** (Kothari Commission, 1964–66) and NEP 2020 emphasise multilingual education while leaving states flexibility. Views differ: supporters stress national communication and mother-tongue learning respectively, critics fear imposition or neglect of English/regional languages.

steps.title: Endangerment
steps.body: UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger records thousands of endangered languages; India has many small languages with few speakers. Documentation, community education and digital tools (Unicode, speech datasets) support maintenance.

steps.title: Code-switching
steps.body: Mixing languages is a skill, not a deficiency.

steps.title: Sex and gender
steps.body: **Sex**: biological characteristics (chromosomes, hormones, anatomy), with natural variation including intersex conditions. **Gender**: social roles, norms and identities. Beauvoir (1949): 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' **Butler** (*Gender Trouble*, 1990): gender is **performative** — constituted by repeated acts. **Crenshaw** (1989): **intersectionality** — overlapping systems (gender, caste, class, race) shape experience. **Patriarchy**: systems privileging men; **Connell**: hegemonic masculinity.

steps.title: Debate
steps.body: Scholars and publics differ on how far gender is socially constructed versus influenced by biology; some feminist and other scholars dispute parts of gender-identity theory. Present positions with their reasons and evidence.

steps.title: Waves
steps.body: Global: first wave (suffrage), second (1960s–80s, equality and bodily autonomy), third (diversity, intersectionality), later digital feminisms. India: reformers (Savitribai Phule, Jyotirao Phule, Pandita Ramabai, Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, Begum), abolition of sati (1829), Widow Remarriage Act (1856), women in the freedom struggle, the 1970s movements (SEWA 1972, anti-rape law reform after Mathura case, Shah Bano debates), Vishakha guidelines (1997) leading to the POSH Act 2013, and the 2012 Delhi gang-rape protests and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013.

steps.title: Pluralism
steps.body: Indian feminisms include Dalit feminism, Muslim women's movements, Adivasi and rural women's organising, with differing priorities.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body: **NALSA v Union of India (2014)**: recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify gender and treated them as a socially and educationally backward class. **Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018)**: read down Section 377 to decriminalise consensual same-sex acts between adults. **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019** (criticised by many activists for its certification provisions). **Supriyo v Union of India (October 2023)**: the Supreme Court declined to recognise a right to same-sex marriage, leaving legislation to Parliament while affirming that transgender persons may marry in heterosexual unions under existing law.

steps.title: Perspectives
steps.body: Supporters of broader recognition cite equality and dignity; some religious and social groups cite tradition and religion; the courts emphasise constitutional morality and separation of powers. Present each position in its own terms.

courses.title: Media & Cultural Studies · power, representation and audiences
courses.summary: Media theory (Frankfurt School, McLuhan, Hall, Anderson), Indian media history, representation, misinformation and media literacy labs.
outcomes: Explain culture industry, medium theory and encoding/decoding
Trace Indian media from Doordarshan to digital platforms

scenes.text: Two viewers read the same poster differently.
Audiences interpret.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body: **Adorno and Horkheimer** (*Dialectic of Enlightenment*, 1947): the 'culture industry' standardises mass culture. **McLuhan** (*Understanding Media*, 1964): 'the medium is the message'. **Gramsci**: hegemony — consent produced through culture. **Stuart Hall** (1973): **encoding/decoding** — dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings. **Anderson** (1983): nations as 'imagined communities' via print capitalism. The Birmingham Centre (CCCS, 1964) founded British cultural studies.

steps.title: Reading types
steps.body: A news item praising a policy: a supporter reads it as intended (dominant), a neutral viewer accepts part (negotiated), a critic rejects the framing (oppositional).

steps.title: Scepticism
steps.body: Theories offer lenses, not laws; audience research shows people are active, not passive.

lessons.title: Indian media: from radio to platforms

scenes.text: In 1982 many Indians watched the Asian Games in colour for the first time.
Technology changed audiences.

steps.title: Timeline
steps.body: All India Radio (named 1936); **Doordarshan** began experimentally in 1959 (Delhi) with national expansion around 1982; satellite and cable TV from 1991; private news channels in the late 1990s; internet and mobile growth, especially after 2016's low-cost data; OTT and short-video platforms; regulation: Press Council of India (1966; current body 1979), Cable Television Networks Act 1995, IT Act 2000 and the IT Rules 2021, Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023.

steps.title: Issues
steps.body: Press freedom, ownership concentration, paid news, polarisation, regional-language media growth. Views differ on regulation versus freedom of expression (Article 19(1)(a), with reasonable restrictions in 19(2)).

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Compare coverage across outlets of varied ownership and orientation.

scenes.text: A forwarded message claims a miracle cure.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Agenda-setting** (McCombs and Shaw, 1972): media influence what we think about. **Framing** shapes how issues are understood. **Representation** studies who appears and how (gender, caste, region, disability). **Misinformation** (false, unintentionally shared) vs **disinformation** (deliberate).

steps.title: Verification
steps.body: Check the source, search for the original, check date and place (reverse image search), look for independent confirmation, check fact-check organisations.

courses.title: History of Science & Technology in India
courses.summary: Mathematics, astronomy, metallurgy, medicine and modern science and space in India from antiquity to ISRO, with attention to sources and dating debates.
outcomes: Describe the place-value system, zero and Aryabhata's contributions
Explain the Kerala school's infinite series
Summarise Indian metallurgy and medicine in sources
Trace modern Indian science and space milestones

scenes.text: A shopkeeper writes 405 and the middle 0 holds the tens place.
Place value changed arithmetic.

steps.title: Place value and zero
steps.body: The decimal place-value system with zero developed in India; the Bakhshali manuscript contains an early dot used as a placeholder (radiocarbon dating of its birch-bark folios gave a range of centuries, with some as early as the 3rd–4th century CE, and the result is debated). **Brahmagupta** (*Brahmasphutasiddhanta*, 628 CE) gave rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers. Numerals spread to the Islamic world and Europe ('Hindu-Arabic numerals').

steps.title: Aryabhata
steps.body: Born 476 CE; *Aryabhatiya* (499 CE): sine tables, an approximation of π as 62832/20000, planetary computations, and the claim that the Earth rotates on its axis (accepted by few successors).

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: 62832 ÷ 20000 = 3.1416, accurate to four decimals (π = 3.14159…).

scenes.text: Madhava found infinite series for trigonometric functions around 1400.
Calculus precursors.

steps.title: Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340–1425)
steps.body: Founded the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics; derived infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent, later known in Europe as Gregory–Leibniz (π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + …). Successors: Nilakantha, Jyeshthadeva (*Yuktibhasha*, c. 1530).

steps.title: Others
steps.body: **Bhaskara II** (1114–c. 1185): *Siddhanta Shiromani* and *Lilavati*; **Jantar Mantar** observatories (Jai Singh II, Jaipur 1734).

steps.title: Careful
steps.body: Historians debate whether Kerala results reached Europe; there is no conclusive evidence of transmission, so independent discovery is the cautious claim.

scenes.text: The Iron Pillar of Delhi, dated to roughly the 4th–5th century CE, shows little corrosion.

steps.title: Metallurgy
steps.body: Wootz steel from southern India was exported widely and associated with 'Damascus' blades; the Delhi Iron Pillar's corrosion resistance has been attributed to a protective passive layer rich in iron hydrogen phosphate, aided by high phosphorus content and the dry climate. Zinc distillation at Zawar in Rajasthan (from about the 12th century) is notable.

steps.title: Medicine
steps.body: **Sushruta Samhita**: surgery, instruments, procedures including nasal reconstruction; **Charaka Samhita**: internal medicine and ethics. Dating is debated; they were compiled over centuries (roughly 1st century BCE–4th century CE for redactions). Ayurveda's modern practice sits alongside biomedicine.

steps.title: Keep evidence-based
steps.body: Claims should be matched to textual or archaeological evidence.

courses.summary: Translation movement, algebra, optics, medicine and astronomy in the Abbasid and wider Islamic world, and its links with Indian, Greek and Chinese knowledge.

scenes.text: Scholars of different faiths translate Greek, Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic.
A multicultural enterprise.

steps.title: Context
steps.body: Under the Abbasids (from 750 CE) Baghdad became a centre of learning; the **House of Wisdom** (Bayt al-Hikma), flourishing under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833), supported translation and research. Paper-making spread west after contact with China (traditionally linked to Samarkand c. 751). Translators included Hunayn ibn Ishaq (a Nestorian Christian).

steps.title: Sources
steps.body: Greek (Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen), Persian, Syriac and Indian (*Siddhanta* astronomy, numerals) works were translated and critiqued.

steps.title: Avoid myths
steps.body: The 'Golden Age' label is a convenience; scholars debate its scope and chronology, and that it was not purely 'Arab' but multi-ethnic and multi-faith.

steps.title: Al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850)

uni-hum-x-phil-india.description: Complete tour of the Indian darshanas — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta, Buddhist, Jain and Charvaka — with debate, comparison and reasoning labs. Each school presented in its own terms.

courses.title: Nyaya & Vaisheshika · knowledge, inference and atoms
courses.summary: The two allied 'realist' darshanas: Nyaya's theory of valid knowledge and debate, and Vaisheshika's categories and atomism. Covers topics commonly taught in university Indian-philosophy courses.
outcomes: Explain the four pramanas of Nyaya and what each justifies

scenes.text: Asha sees the road is wet and wonders: rain, or a water tanker?
Nyaya says the question 'how do I know?' deserves a rigorous answer, not a shrug.

steps.title: Nyaya and its method
steps.body: Nyaya is traditionally traced to the **Nyaya Sutras** attributed to Gautama (also called Akshapada). Its project is epistemological first: identify the **pramanas** (means of valid knowledge) and use them to test claims about the world and the self. Nyaya is a *realist* school: the world exists independently of our minds and can be known.

steps.title: The four pramanas
steps.body:
- **Pratyaksha** (perception): knowledge from sense-object contact, free of error.
- **Anumana** (inference): knowledge from a mark, e.g. smoke → fire.
- **Upamana** (comparison/analogy): knowing a thing by its similarity to a described thing, e.g. 'a gavaya is like a cow'.
- **Shabda** (reliable testimony): the word of a trustworthy person or scripture.

steps.title: Schools differ on the count
steps.body: Charvaka accepts only perception; Vaisheshika and the Buddhist logicians Dignaga and Dharmakirti accept perception and inference; Samkhya adds testimony; Mimamsa and Advaita accept more (Kumarila and Advaita: six, adding arthapatti and anupalabdhi). Don't state 'Indian philosophy has four pramanas' as if universal.

scenes.text: A traveller sees smoke rising from a far hill.
He reasons 'there is fire' — and Nyaya shows how to lay that reasoning out so a sceptic can test it.

steps.title: The five members (avayava)
steps.body:
1. **Pratijna** (thesis): The hill has fire.
2. **Hetu** (reason): Because it has smoke.
3. **Udaharana** (example): Whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen hearth.
4. **Upanaya** (application): This hill has smoke of that kind.
5. **Nigamana** (conclusion): Therefore the hill has fire.

steps.title: Vyapti: the invariable link
steps.body: The engine of inference is **vyapti**, the pervasion between reason and probandum: wherever smoke, there fire. Terms: **paksha** (subject: hill), **sadhya** (what is to be proved: fire), **hetu/linga** (mark: smoke). How do we know vyapti is universal? Nyaya appeals to repeated observation with no counter-case, plus tarka (hypothetical reasoning). Critics, notably the Charvakas, say this never reaches certainty — a version of the problem of induction.

steps.title: Kinds of inference
steps.body: Later Nyaya lists **purvavat** (cause→effect), **sheshavat** (effect→cause, e.g. a swollen river → rain upstream) and **samanyatodrishta** (by general correlation). Navya-Nyaya (from Gangesha, around the 13th–14th century) refined this with a precise technical language.

scenes.text: Kiran watches dust motes in a sunbeam and asks what the smallest piece could be.

steps.title: Padarthas (categories)
steps.body: The Vaisheshika Sutras (Kanada) list **dravya** (substance), **guna** (quality), **karma** (action), **samanya** (universal), **vishesha** (particularity) and **samavaya** (inherence). Later authors (e.g. Shridhara, Udayana) add **abhava** (absence) as a seventh.

steps.title: Nine substances
steps.body: Earth, water, fire, air, ether (akasha), time, space, self (atman) and mind (manas). The first four have atomic (paramanu) forms; ether, time, space and self are all-pervading; mind is atomic in size. Composite objects arise from atoms: two atoms → dyad (dvyanuka), three dyads → triad (tryanuka), the first visible unit.

steps.title: Not modern atomic theory
steps.body: Vaisheshika atomism is a *metaphysical* and logical argument (a regress of divisibility must stop), not an experimental theory. Compare it with Greek atomism (Democritus) with respect, but avoid claiming it 'anticipated' modern physics.

steps.title: Five hetvabhasas
steps.body:
- **Savyabhichara** (erratic): reason is found both where the probandum is present and where it is absent.
- **Viruddha** (contradictory): reason proves the opposite.
- **Prakaranasama / satpratipaksha** (counterbalanced): an equally strong reason proves the contrary.
- **Asiddha / sadhyasama** (unestablished): reason itself is not established in the subject.
- **Kalatita / badhita** (mistimed/sublated): the claim is already contradicted by a stronger pramana.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 'Sound is eternal because it is an object of knowledge.' Pots are also objects of knowledge and non-eternal, so the reason occurs where the probandum is absent: **savyabhichara**.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1) Identify paksha, sadhya, hetu. 2) Test vyapti: is there a counter-example? 3) Check the hetu is present in the paksha. 4) Check no stronger pramana already settles it.

steps.title: Classical Samkhya
steps.body: Systematised in Ishvarakrishna's **Samkhya Karika** (around the 4th–5th century CE), with Kapila as traditional founder. It is *dualist*: **purusha** (many conscious, passive witnesses) and **prakriti** (one unconscious, productive nature). Suffering arises from non-discrimination (aviveka) between them; liberation (kaivalya) is discriminative knowledge.

steps.title: Arguments for prakriti
steps.body: The Karika argues from the finite nature of effects, their shared character, and *satkaryavada*: the effect pre-exists in the cause in latent form, as oil in sesame seeds.

steps.title: Avoid a common error
steps.body: Classical Samkhya is usually described as non-theistic (no creator-God), though Yoga adds Ishvara. Treat labels like 'atheist' with nuance: Samkhya counts as an orthodox (astika) school.

steps.title: Three gunas
steps.body: **Sattva** (clarity, lightness), **rajas** (activity, passion), **tamas** (inertia, obscurity). Prakriti is their equilibrium; its disturbance sets evolution going.

steps.title: The 25 tattvas
steps.body: Purusha and prakriti, then from prakriti: **buddhi (mahat)**, **ahamkara**, **manas**, five **jnanendriyas**, five **karmendriyas**, five **tanmatras** and five **mahabhutas**.

steps.title: Yoga darshana
steps.body: The **Yoga Sutras** of Patanjali (dating debated, commonly placed between the 2nd century BCE and the 4th century CE) define yoga as *chitta-vritti-nirodha* — stilling the fluctuations of the mind. The metaphysics follows Samkhya but admits **Ishvara** as a special purusha.

steps.title: Eight limbs
steps.body: **Yama** (restraints), **niyama** (observances), **asana** (posture), **pranayama** (breath regulation), **pratyahara** (withdrawal), **dharana** (concentration), **dhyana** (meditation), **samadhi** (absorption).

steps.title: Modern yoga

steps.title: Jaimini and dharma
steps.body: The **Mimamsa Sutras** (attributed to Jaimini) open by defining dharma as what is indicated by **codana**, the Vedic injunction. Mimamsa is the study of how to interpret Vedic sentences, which makes it a rich philosophy of language, hermeneutics and ritual action.

steps.title: Two sub-schools and key theses
steps.body: **Prabhakara** and **Kumarila Bhatta** (c. 7th century) differ on details. Shared theses: the Veda is *apaurusheya* (authorless/not composed by any person); knowledge is intrinsically valid until a defeater appears (*svatah pramanya*); the relation between word and meaning is natural. Classical Mimamsa was largely unconcerned with a creator-God and focused on ritual duty.

steps.title: Don't conflate
steps.body: Purva Mimamsa (earlier: ritual portion) is distinct from Uttara Mimamsa, which is another name for Vedanta (later: Upanishadic portion).

steps.title: Prasthanatrayi
steps.body: The 'triple canon': the **Upanishads**, the **Brahma Sutras** (Badarayana) and the **Bhagavad Gita**. Each school writes a *bhashya* (commentary) on all three, which is how doctrine is argued.

steps.title: The key question
steps.body: Upanishadic statements like *tat tvam asi* ('you are that') and *aham brahmasmi* sound like identity of self and Brahman, while others speak of a Lord distinct from souls. Schools resolve this differently.

steps.title: Three major acharyas
steps.body: **Adi Shankara** (traditionally c. 8th century CE) — Advaita; **Ramanuja** (traditionally 1017–1137) — Vishishtadvaita; **Madhva** (1238–1317) — Dvaita. Dating of Shankara is debated by scholars.

steps.title: Advaita (Shankara)
steps.body: Only **Brahman** (pure being-consciousness, *nirguna*) is ultimately real; the individual self is not different from Brahman; the world is a superimposition (*adhyasa*) due to **avidya/maya**, like the snake on the rope. Liberation = knowledge (*jnana*) of non-difference. Critics (Ramanuja) ask: whose ignorance, and how can pure consciousness be ignorant?

steps.title: Vishishtadvaita (Ramanuja)
steps.body: Brahman is Vishnu/Narayana with attributes; souls and matter are real but are the **body** of Brahman — a differentiated unity. Path: devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*).

steps.title: Dvaita (Madhva)
steps.body: Five real, eternal differences: God–soul, God–matter, soul–soul, soul–matter, matter–matter. God (Vishnu) is independent; souls are dependent. Grace and devotion matter.

steps.title: Writing tip
steps.body: Present each as an internally coherent answer to the same questions: What is ultimately real? How is the self related to Brahman? What is the world? How is liberation reached?

lessons.title: The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path

scenes.text: Zara wonders why wanting more never seems to end.
The Buddha is traditionally said to have framed this as a diagnosis and treatment.

steps.title: Four Noble Truths
steps.body:
1. **Dukkha**: life includes unsatisfactoriness and suffering.
2. **Samudaya**: its origin is craving/clinging (*tanha*).
3. **Nirodha**: its cessation (nirvana) is possible.
4. **Magga**: the path leading to cessation.

steps.title: Eightfold Path
steps.body: Wisdom (*prajna*): right view, right intention. Ethics (*sila*): right speech, right action, right livelihood. Concentration (*samadhi*): right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

steps.title: Schools
steps.body: Theravada (Pali canon; Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia), Mahayana (Chinese, Japanese, Tibetan, Korean traditions; bodhisattva ideal) and Vajrayana. Traditional dates of the Buddha vary; scholars commonly place his life in the 5th century BCE ± several decades.

steps.title: Three marks
steps.body: **Anicca** (impermanence), **dukkha**, **anatta** (non-self): no permanent, unchanging essence in what we call a person. The person is analysed into five aggregates (*skandhas*): form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness.

steps.title: Pratityasamutpada
steps.body: Everything arises dependent on conditions. The 12-link chain: ignorance → formations → consciousness → name-and-form → six sense bases → contact → feeling → craving → clinging → becoming → birth → ageing and death.

steps.title: Anatta is not nihilism
steps.body: Buddhist schools deny a permanent self but affirm moral continuity (karma, rebirth in traditional views). Hindu schools such as Nyaya and Advaita argue against anatta; present both fairly.

scenes.text: Monks debate whether things have inherent nature.

steps.title: Madhyamaka
steps.body: **Nagarjuna** (c. 2nd–3rd century CE) argued in the *Mulamadhyamakakarika* that things lack **svabhava** (intrinsic nature): they are *empty* (*shunya*) because dependently arisen. Emptiness is not nothingness; it is the 'middle way' between eternalism and nihilism. Two truths: conventional and ultimate.

steps.title: Yogacara
steps.body: **Asanga** and **Vasubandhu** (4th–5th century CE): experience is structured by consciousness (*vijnapti-matra*, 'representation-only'), with store-consciousness (*alaya-vijnana*). Interpretations vary: idealism vs epistemological claim.

steps.title: Dignaga and Dharmakirti
steps.body: Only two pramanas: **perception** (free from conceptual construction) and **inference**. Dignaga (c. 5th–6th century) and Dharmakirti (c. 7th century) developed the theory of *apoha* (meaning by exclusion) and a trairupya (three-aspect) criterion for a valid reason.

steps.title: Anekantavada
steps.body: Reality has infinite aspects; any single statement captures only one standpoint (*naya*). It is a principle of epistemic humility and of non-violence in thought.

steps.title: Syadvada and saptabhangi
steps.body: Each assertion is qualified by *syat* ('in some respect'). Seven-fold predication: syad asti (exists), syad nasti (does not exist), syad asti-nasti, syad avaktavya (inexpressible), and three combinations with inexpressibility: 7 forms total.

steps.body: Jiva (soul), pudgala (matter), dharma (medium of motion), adharma (medium of rest), akasha (space), kala (time). Souls are many, conscious and every living thing has one.

steps.title: Karma and liberation
steps.body: Karma is subtle matter that binds the soul; liberation (*moksha*) by the **three jewels**: right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Five **mahavratas**: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya, aparigraha.

courses.title: Ancient Greek Philosophy · from Thales to the Hellenistic schools
courses.summary: The Pre-Socratics, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and the Hellenistic schools (Epicureans, Stoics, Sceptics), with primary-text reading skills.

scenes.text: Around 400 BCE a man stops people and asks 'what is courage?'
Socrates began where earlier thinkers had left off: from the cosmos to the examined life.

steps.title: First questions
steps.body: **Thales** (c. 624–546 BCE) proposed water as the underlying stuff; **Anaximander** the *apeiron* (boundless); **Heraclitus** emphasised change ('you cannot step into the same river twice'); **Parmenides** argued that change is impossible and that what-is is one. **Democritus** posited atoms and void.

steps.title: Socrates (470–399 BCE)
steps.body: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes. His **elenchus** tests definitions through question and answer, exposing contradictions. He was tried for impiety and corrupting the young and executed in 399 BCE.

steps.title: The Socratic problem
steps.body: Which views belong to the historical Socrates and which to Plato's character? Scholars treat early Platonic dialogues as closer to Socrates.

lessons.title: Plato: Forms, the Cave and the soul

scenes.text: Prisoners in a cave think shadows are everything.
Plato's Republic uses this to explain knowledge.

steps.title: Theory of Forms
steps.body: The Forms (e.g. Beauty, Justice, Equal) are eternal, non-material, perfect patterns; physical things *participate* in them. Knowledge (*episteme*) is of Forms; opinion (*doxa*) is of changing things.

steps.title: Allegory of the Cave (Republic VII)
steps.body: Prisoners chained see only shadows; the freed prisoner gradually sees the sun, i.e. the Form of the Good. The philosopher must return to educate others. Tripartite soul: reason, spirit, appetite; a just city mirrors a just soul.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: Aristotle (and Plato himself in the *Parmenides*) raises the 'third man' problem: if a Form explains similarity, what explains the similarity between Form and particulars?

steps.title: Virtue ethics and logic
steps.body: In the *Nicomachean Ethics* the aim is **eudaimonia** (flourishing), achieved through virtues as a mean between extremes, guided by practical wisdom (*phronesis*). In the *Organon* Aristotle systematised the **syllogism**: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal.

scenes.text: Aarav wonders if everything he sees could be a dream.

steps.title: Method of doubt
steps.body: René Descartes (1596–1650) doubts anything that can be doubted: the senses, the external world (dreaming), even mathematics (evil demon). One thing survives: **'I think, therefore I am'** (*cogito*; Discourse 1637, Meditations 1641).

steps.title: Rationalists
steps.body: Descartes, **Spinoza** (monism: God or Nature) and **Leibniz** (monads; principle of sufficient reason) hold reason is the chief source of knowledge, with innate ideas.

steps.title: Mind–body problem
steps.body: Descartes' dualism faces the interaction problem: how does an immaterial mind move a body? Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him on it in correspondence.

steps.title: Empiricism
steps.body: **Locke** (1632–1704): no innate ideas; ideas come from sensation and reflection; primary vs secondary qualities. **Berkeley** (1685–1753): *esse est percipi*, to be is to be perceived. **Hume** (1711–1776): all ideas derive from impressions.

steps.title: Hume's two problems
steps.body: **Induction**: no non-circular justification that the future will resemble the past. **Causation**: we observe constant conjunction, never a necessary connection. **Hume's fork**: all knowledge concerns relations of ideas (logic, mathematics) or matters of fact (experience).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 'The sun will rise tomorrow' is a matter of fact: denying it is not self-contradictory, so only experience supports it, and experience of the past cannot prove the future without assuming uniformity of nature.

steps.title: The question
steps.body: Hume woke Kant 'from his dogmatic slumber'. Kant's *Critique of Pure Reason* (1781; 2nd ed. 1787) asks: how are **synthetic a priori** judgements possible (e.g. '7 + 5 = 12', 'every event has a cause')?

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The mind contributes the forms of intuition (space, time) and twelve categories (e.g. causality, substance). We know **phenomena** (things as they appear), never **noumena** (things in themselves). Reason oversteps in 'antinomies'.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: The **categorical imperative**: act only on maxims you could will as universal law; treat humanity never merely as a means but always also as an end. Duty from good will, not consequences.

courses.summary: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, Husserl and Heidegger, Sartre, Beauvoir and Camus: philosophies of existence, freedom and meaning.

scenes.text: A graduate must choose a path with no guarantees.

steps.title: Kierkegaard (1813–1855)
steps.body: Danish thinker; the self is a task; stages of existence (aesthetic, ethical, religious); the 'leap of faith' and anxiety as the dizziness of freedom. Often called the father of existentialism.

steps.title: Nietzsche (1844–1900)
steps.body: Declared 'God is dead' (*The Gay Science*, 1882) as a diagnosis of Europe's loss of foundations, not a celebration; proposed revaluing values, the *Übermensch*, will to power and eternal recurrence as a test of affirmation.

steps.title: Misreadings
steps.body: Nietzsche's work was distorted by later political movements; scholars stress his criticism of nationalism and antisemitism.

scenes.text: Describe the cup as it appears, without assumptions.
That is the phenomenological attitude.

steps.title: Husserl (1859–1938)
steps.body: Phenomenology studies experience as it appears. Key moves: **epoché** (bracketing assumptions about the external world) and **intentionality** (consciousness is always of something).

steps.title: Heidegger (1889–1976)
steps.body: *Being and Time* (1927) asks the question of being. **Dasein** (human existence) is being-in-the-world, always already involved with tools and others; **being-towards-death** makes authentic existence possible. Heidegger's membership of the Nazi party (1933) remains a serious moral controversy for assessing his work.

steps.title: Reading tip
steps.body: Use the glossary; Heidegger's terms are technical.

scenes.text: Sartre describes a waiter acting too perfectly 'waiter-like'.

steps.title: Sartre (1905–1980)
steps.body: *Being and Nothingness* (1943): **existence precedes essence** — no fixed human nature; we are 'condemned to be free' and responsible. **Bad faith** denies freedom by hiding behind roles or circumstances.

steps.title: Beauvoir (1908–1986)
steps.body: *The Second Sex* (1949): 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' — analysing how social situations shape women's freedom; ethics of ambiguity.

steps.title: Camus (1913–1960)
steps.body: *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942): the **absurd** is the clash between our demand for meaning and the silent world; he rejects suicide and religious leaps and recommends revolt. Camus rejected the 'existentialist' label.

scenes.text: The morning star and evening star are the same planet, yet 'they are identical' is informative.

steps.title: Frege (1848–1925)

courses.summary: A respectful, factual introduction to the diversity of Hindu traditions, scriptures, concepts and practices. Describes beliefs as adherents themselves state them, with academic history alongside; it takes no position on theological truth.

scenes.text: Neha's grandmother worships Vishnu, her neighbour Shiva, a friend the Goddess.
All might be called Hindu — yet no single founder or creed unites them.

steps.title: What 'Hindu' means
steps.body: The word *Hindu* originally derived from the Sanskritised/Persian name for the Indus (Sindhu). Today the term covers diverse traditions with no single founder, central authority or creed. Adherents often prefer *Sanatana Dharma* ('eternal order'); scholars also use 'Hindu traditions'.

steps.title: Major traditions
steps.body: **Vaishnavism** (Vishnu and avatars such as Rama and Krishna), **Shaivism** (Shiva), **Shaktism** (the Goddess), **Smartism** (worship of five deities, associated with Advaita). Many Hindus also follow regional, village and family traditions.

steps.title: Avoid stereotypes
steps.body: Hinduism is neither simply 'polytheistic' nor simply 'monotheistic': positions range from monism (Advaita) to devotional theism to non-theistic schools (Samkhya, Mimamsa). Say 'many Hindus believe…' rather than 'Hindus believe…'.

lessons.title: Texts: from the Vedas to the Gita

steps.title: Shruti and smriti

steps.title: Dating
steps.body: The Rigveda is generally dated to around 1500–1000 BCE; the early Upanishads to around 800–500 BCE; the epics reached their present form over several centuries around the turn of the era. Dates are approximate and debated.

steps.title: The Gita
steps.body: A dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna set before the Kurukshetra battle; discusses duty (karma yoga), knowledge (jnana yoga) and devotion (bhakti yoga). Interpreted differently by Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and others.

steps.title: Concepts

steps.title: Foundations
steps.body: Muhammad (c. 570–632 CE) is regarded by Muslims as the final prophet. The **Hijra** (migration from Mecca to Medina, 622 CE) marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar. The Quran is held to be the word of God, revealed in Arabic.

steps.title: Six articles of faith
steps.body: Belief in God (Allah, strictly one: *tawhid*), angels, scripture, prophets (including Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa), the Last Day and divine decree (*qadar*).

steps.title: Five pillars
steps.body: **Shahada** (declaration of faith), **salat** (five daily prayers), **zakat** (obligatory charity), **sawm** (fasting in Ramadan), **hajj** (pilgrimage to Mecca once in life if able).

steps.title: Schools
steps.body: Four Sunni schools of law (*madhhabs*): Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali; Shia Ja'fari school. In India the Hanafi school is most widespread among Sunnis. Interpretation (*ijtihad*) and the scope of Sharia as law vs ethics are debated among Muslims.

steps.title: Sunni and Shia

Sunnis (majority, roughly 85–90% worldwide) accept the early caliphs; Shia revere Ali and the Imams (Twelver, Ismaili and Zaydi branches). steps.title: Sufism

steps.title: India
steps.body: Islam arrived via Arab traders on the Malabar coast (7th century onward), and later through Central Asian dynasties. India has one of the world's largest Muslim populations; communities include Sunni, Shia, Bohra, Khoja, Ahmadiyya (whose status is disputed by many Muslims), and many regional cultures.

steps.title: Guru Nanak (1469–1539)
steps.body: Born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). Taught **Ik Onkar** (One God), equality of all people, honest living and remembering God. His journeys (*udasis*) are central in Sikh memory. He settled at Kartarpur.

steps.title: The ten Gurus
steps.body: Nanak, Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, Gobind Singh. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth (1604) and built Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple, Amritsar); Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the eternal Guru (1708).

steps.title: Historical note

steps.title: Guru Granth Sahib
steps.body: 1,430 pages (angs) in Gurmukhi containing compositions by Sikh Gurus and by saints of various backgrounds, including Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid. Installed with great reverence as the living Guru.

steps.title: Gurdwara and langar
steps.body: A gurdwara ('door of the Guru') houses the scripture; everyone is welcome, heads covered, shoes off. **Langar** is the free community kitchen; **seva** is selfless service.

steps.title: Three pillars
steps.body: **Naam japna** (remembering God), **kirat karni** (honest work), **vand chakna** (sharing).

steps.title: Diversity
steps.body: Not all Sikhs are amritdhari; many (including *sehajdhari*) follow the Gurus' teaching without full initiation. In India Sikhs are about 1.7% of the population (2011 Census), concentrated in Punjab.

steps.title: Misconceptions
steps.body: Sikhism is a distinct religion, not a sect of Hinduism or Islam; the turban is a religious article of faith, not a cultural costume; the kirpan is a religious article, with legal accommodations in India under Article 25.

steps.body: Jews trace their story to Abraham, Moses and the covenant. The **Tanakh** (Hebrew Bible: Torah, Prophets, Writings) and the **Talmud** (rabbinic discussion) are central. The Torah comprises five books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy.

steps.body: Indian Jewish communities include the Bene Israel (Konkan), Cochin Jews (Kerala; the Paradesi Synagogue of 1568) and Baghdadi Jews (Kolkata, Mumbai). Their numbers today are small; their history is generally described as one of peaceful coexistence.

steps.title: Teachings
steps.body: Founded by **Zarathustra (Zoroaster)**, whose date is debated (roughly 1500–1000 BCE by many scholars). Scripture: **Avesta** (including the Gathas). Worship of **Ahura Mazda**; the moral ethic **good thoughts, good words, good deeds** (*humata, hukhta, hvarshta*); the struggle of truth (*asha*) against falsehood (*druj*). Fire is a symbol of purity, used in fire temples.

steps.title: Parsis in India
steps.body: Parsis, Persian Zoroastrians who settled in Gujarat (traditionally from the 8th–10th centuries per the *Qissa-i Sanjan*), became prominent in trade and industry (Tata, Godrej, Wadia families) and public life. Navroz marks the new year. Their population is declining, an issue of community concern; the Government of India has run the Parzor/Jiyo Parsi initiative.

uni-hum-x-society.description: Sociology of caste, class, gender, family, urbanisation and social movements in India, plus social-cultural anthropology, using data and balanced scholarly debate.

lessons.title: Varna, jati and the sociological view

scenes.text: A researcher records dozens of jatis in a single village but only four varnas in the texts.
Sociologists separate textual ideals from lived structure.

steps.title: Varna and jati
steps.body: **Varna** is the fourfold textual classification (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra). **Jati** is the endogamous, hereditary local group, numbering in thousands, tied to occupation, rank and marriage. Outside the varna scheme, 'Dalits' (formerly 'untouchables') faced exclusion; Scheduled Castes are the legal category.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: **Louis Dumont** (*Homo Hierarchicus*, 1966): caste is a ritual hierarchy of purity and pollution. **M. N. Srinivas** stressed dominance and mobility. **Ambedkar** (*Annihilation of Caste*, 1936) argued caste is a social order sustained by scriptural sanction and demanded its annihilation. Others (e.g. Nicholas Dirks) argue colonial census and administration hardened caste categories; critics reply that caste long predates colonialism.

steps.title: Care
steps.body: Avoid saying caste 'was invented by the British' or 'is just religion'; scholarship shows both pre-colonial roots and colonial transformation.

scenes.text: A community adopts vegetarianism and Brahmanical rites to claim higher rank.
Srinivas called this Sanskritisation.

steps.title: Sanskritisation
steps.body: Coined by M. N. Srinivas (in his study of the Coorgs, 1952): a lower caste adopts customs of higher castes to raise its status. Criticisms: it describes reference-group mobility, not structural change; Dalit movements often reject it (e.g. conversion, assertion of identity).

steps.title: Dominant caste
steps.body: A numerically strong, economically and politically powerful landowning caste in a village (e.g. Okkaligas, Jats, Patidars, Marathas in various regions). Other processes: **Westernisation**, **modernisation**, **de-Sanskritisation**.

steps.title: Legal change
steps.body: Article 17 abolished untouchability; the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 provide remedies.

quiz.q: Which Act (1989) addresses atrocities on SC/ST?

scenes.text: Ravi's father drove a truck; Ravi studies engineering.

steps.title: Class theories
steps.body: **Marx**: class defined by relation to means of production. **Weber**: class (market position), status (honour) and party (power). **Bourdieu**: economic, cultural and social capital shape reproduction of advantage.

steps.title: Reservation framework
steps.body: Articles 15(4), 16(4) allow special provisions. Central reservation: **SC 15%**, **ST 7.5%**, **OBC 27%** (after Mandal Commission report 1980, implemented in 1990; upheld in *Indra Sawhney* 1992 with a 50% general ceiling and creamy layer exclusion). **EWS 10%** introduced by the 103rd Amendment (2019), upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022. Views differ: supporters stress corrective justice and representation; critics raise efficiency, creamy-layer and caste-versus-economic-criterion concerns; empirical research on outcomes is mixed.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: 15 + 7.5 + 27 = 49.5%; adding EWS 10% gives 59.5%, which exceeds the 50% ceiling that applied to earlier categories; the 2022 judgment held EWS is a separate category not violating the basic structure.

courses.title: Gender, Family and Marriage in India
courses.summary: Sociological study of gender, family structures, marriage law and women's status in India, using Census and survey data and several scholarly perspectives.
outcomes: Distinguish joint and nuclear families and the debates around them
Read sex-ratio data and compute indicators
Summarise key laws on marriage, dowry and domestic violence

scenes.text: Three generations eat from one kitchen in a Pune apartment.
Joint families adapt to urban life.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Joint family** (I. P. Desai: joint property, commensality, mutual obligations), **nuclear**, **extended**. Research (Shah, Desai) shows joint families are fluid, with 'functional jointness' even when households are separate. Descent: mostly patrilineal; matrilineal groups include the Khasi, Garo and historically the Nairs.

steps.title: Change
steps.body: Migration, nuclearisation, ageing and women's employment reshape households. Census 2011 reports average household size about 4.8.

steps.title: Terminology
steps.body: Use household (residence) and family (kin) as distinct concepts.

lessons.title: Sex ratio and women's status: reading the data

scenes.text: A district's child sex ratio is far below the state average.
What do the numbers show?

steps.title: Indicators
steps.body: Sex ratio = females per 1000 males. India (Census 2011): **943**; child sex ratio (0–6 years): **919**, the lowest since Independence at that time. Kerala has the highest overall (1084). NFHS-5 (2019–21) reports a sex ratio at birth of about 929 births and a total fertility rate of 2.0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: In a village with 5,000 males and a sex ratio of 943, expected females = 5,000 × 943 / 1000 = **4,715**.

steps.title: Explanations
steps.body: Son preference, sex-selective abortion (PCPNDT Act 1994 prohibits sex determination), neglect of girls, migration; improvements with education and policy such as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015). Scholars (Amartya Sen's 'missing women' thesis) highlight discrimination.

steps.title: Practices
steps.body: Arranged marriage predominates, with caste and community endogamy; the share of love or self-choice marriages is rising in urban areas. Child marriage is prohibited: Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 (minimum ages 18 for women and 21 for men).

steps.title: Key laws
steps.body: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 and Hindu Succession Act 1956 (amended 2005: daughters equal coparceners), Special Marriage Act 1954 (inter-faith/inter-caste), Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005. Personal laws vary by religion; debates about a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) present contrasting views on equality, pluralism and religious freedom.

steps.title: Women's reservation
steps.body: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and state-assembly seats for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

steps.title: Fields
steps.body: Social-cultural, biological (physical), archaeological and linguistic anthropology. Key ideas: **culture** (learned, shared patterns), **cultural relativism** (understand beliefs in their context, which is not the same as moral approval of everything), **ethnocentrism** (judging others by one's own standards).

steps.title: Fieldwork
steps.body: **Participant observation**, interviews, genealogies, field notes. **Clifford Geertz**: 'thick description' (1973) interprets the meaning of actions, as in the wink versus the twitch.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Informed consent, confidentiality, avoiding harm; anthropology's colonial history is openly debated.

steps.title: Kinship
steps.body: Descent: patrilineal, matrilineal, bilateral. Rules: **endogamy** (marry within a group), **exogamy** (outside). **Irawati Karve**, *Kinship Organisation in India* (1953), mapped regional kinship systems including the contrast between northern and southern marriage rules.

steps.title: Exchange
steps.body: **Mauss**, *The Gift* (1925): gifts create obligations (give, receive, reciprocate). **Sahlins**: generalised, balanced, negative reciprocity. **Lévi-Strauss**: alliance theory, marriage as exchange of women between groups (criticised by feminist anthropologists).

steps.title: Reciprocity
steps.body: A neighbour who lends rice and is repaid later practises balanced reciprocity; a gift to a child with no expectation is generalised.

steps.title: Rites of passage

Srinivas (Coorgs, Rampura), the Anthropological Survey of India (1945), L. P. Vidyarthi (sacred complex of Gaya). The ‘tribe’ category and Adivasi self-description are themselves debated topics.
